101	## Decision Outcome
102	
103	Chosen option: **C**, because it is the only option measured to honour both halves of Kent's direction — an exact core, and the time model kept — at a cost that leaves the range, the locality proof and the wire shapes intact, and because it is the only one that hands stack 06 the event times the trade needs.
104	
105	### What a number means
106	
107	**A claim's number is the chance it resolves YES by its own deadline.** That is what the sentence on the tile already says. It is not a snapshot read on one day, and **an event that has happened never un-happens**.
108	
109	### Where the time model lives — unchanged
110	
111	On the arrow. `strength`, `lag`, `shape` and `half_life` keep their names and their meanings. What changes is what they bend: a **rate** — how likely the claim is to happen on each day — instead of a likelihood read on one day. The claim's number is that rate added up across its window.
112	
113	One good thing falls out. An impulse's whole area now counts, so the answer no longer depends on where a deadline happens to fall against a half-life. That is the wart record 0014 admitted, and it is gone: impulse arrows with half-lives of one and two days landing four days before a deadline were attacked deliberately and gave gaps of `.0000` to `.0001` (red-team report §4).
114	
115	*Where the two numbers on an arrow come from is not settled here.* Today the model states an abstract `strength` and our prompt anchors it with a sentence we invented. Kent has decided (2026-09-21) that the claim's own number is asked as *the chance it happens by its deadline if none of the causes on this map happens*, and each arrow as *the chance if this cause happens at the start of the window and no other cause does*, with our code deriving the weight. That change moves what we ask the model, so it lands in the one shape freeze at the end of stack 05 and amends record 0006, not this record.
116	
117	### How it is worked out — two passes
118	
119	1. **One forward pass gives *when*.** Causes first, each claim's chance of having happened by each of 12–24 points across its window. A **Suppose this is true** pins its claim to the day it was supposed and the pass is redone. A claim's yes/no table is then its rate averaged over when its causes arrived.
120	2. **Variable elimination gives *whether*, exactly.** The claims are yes/no, so the whole joint is solved by multiplying the small tables and summing out one claim at a time. **Suppose this is true** replaces a claim's table with a point and cuts its incoming arrows; **This happened** multiplies in an indicator and renormalises. The versions of the map ride along as an array axis, so a whole range is one pass.
121	3. **The worlds the trade needs are drawn on top:** sample truths from the exact joint, then sample each true claim's arrival day forward. Nothing ever conditions on a time, so no inference over times is needed.
122	
123	Two properties stop being machinery and become facts. **Locality becomes a theorem** — a claim cut off from the evidence gets its prior back bit for bit, because its factor sums to one. And **the width shares (FR-21, where more homework would pay) become exact** — re-solve with one stated range frozen, one extra solve each.
124	
125	### The one thing not yet settled: how *This happened* is computed
126	
127	The spike that opens stack 05 measures three candidates against the enumerator that integrates over event times, on the adversarial maps above.
128	
129	* **(a) A weighted forward sample.** Draw worlds forward *with times* — the sampler stack 06 needs anyway — and weight each by how well it matches the evidence. It integrates over *when* correctly, so it converges on the right answer; its cost is sampling noise, and only on observation branches. This is Kent's *"exact core with a sampler on top"* read literally, and it is the recommendation going in.
130	* **(b) Accept the prior-timing tables** and print an observation's numbers to the tolerance measured.
131	* **(c) Re-cut the yes/no variable per evidence day.** Larger tables; may be exact; may be slow.
132	
133	**Kill criterion, fixed before the measuring starts:** if no candidate holds `.005` on 99% of the adversarial set inside 300 ms on a 20-claim map, this design is not adopted as it stands and Kent is told with the numbers.

148	### What `World.series` now means — the largest change hiding in the smallest field
149	
150	Today `series` is a per-day likelihood that is allowed to **fall**, and the golden test pins exactly that (`backend/tests/unit/fixtures/test_hormuz_golden.py:117-120`): the supposed strait claim reads `1.0` on day zero, about `.36` on days one and three, and below `.10` on day four — `1.0 → .36 → .36 → <.10`.

161	
162	The first draft of this design removed it, on the grounds that the path product was its only reader. It is not. Three readers, all live:

170	### Chains are worked out, not multiplied — the path product's replacement
171	
172	This is Kent's decision of 2026-09-21 and it rides here because it needs the exact core to exist.
173	
174	**Why the product goes.** Multiplying likelihoods along a route is not the chance of anything once two claims on the map share a cause. Check it in one line: if a second claim is true exactly when the first is, and both stand at `.5`, the product of the route says `.25`; the chance that every step goes right is `.5`. The product is also read at a different day for every claim on the route, which is the wart record 0014 admitted at its section E.
175	
176	**What replaces it**, three quantities, each a probability or a difference of probabilities, each one or two extra solves:
177	
178	| | What it is |
179	|---|---|
180	| **the shift** | how much the hypothesis moves the destination: the destination's chance with the hypothesis supposed true, minus its chance with the hypothesis supposed false |
181	| **the joint** | the chance every step on the named route goes right — a real joint, from one elimination that keeps the route |
182	| **the weakest arrow** | which single arrow carries most of the shift, and how much of the shift goes with it |
183	
184	What the Verify door then says, *in an illustrative shape only — the real numbers come from the engine at the flip and are owned by the generated numbers file*:

186	> *"Reopening moves the Brent claim by 32 points, from .24 to .56. Every step on the best-backed route goes right in 19% of worlds. The arrow carrying most of that shift is 'reopening → shipping recovers'; delete it and 71% of the effect goes."*

188	**INV-8 becomes:** *"Chains are worked out, not multiplied. Any displayed path shows the shift the hypothesis makes to its destination, the chance every step on it goes right computed as a joint, and which single arrow carries most of the shift."* FR-11, which requires *"the product of link probabilities beside the narrative headline"*, is rewritten to match. Both edits are listed for the pull request that carries this record.

208	### Consequences
209	
210	* Good, because the number on a tile finally answers the sentence beside it, and **This happened** does something.
211	* Good, because supposing any cause on the Hormuz map now moves what that cause points at — defect 2 was the flagship demonstration's quietest failure.
212	* Good, because locality stops being careful bookkeeping and becomes a property of the arithmetic, and the oracle that checks it can get **stricter**.
213	* Good, because the range stops carrying coin-flip width: with every stated range frozen to a point, the band is zero by construction rather than within a tolerance.
214	* Good, because the trade in stack 06 gets a forward sample of *when*, which nothing today produces.
215	* Bad, because **every number on the map changes once**. That is why the flip is a pull request of its own whose review is the diff of one generated file.
216	* Bad, because *This happened* is exact arithmetic on a table built from timing worked out before the evidence — accurate to `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened*>>` and not to machine precision — and the screen prints two significant figures. Whatever the spike returns, the second figure's honesty is stated in the Inspector in words.
217	* Bad, because the induced width of a *generated* map has never been measured: the one real generated map is a tree. Mitigation: at width 7 the exact core is `1.7 ms` on a 30-claim map, four orders of magnitude of headroom; if a pathological map ever appears, fall back to the forward sampler stack 06 uses anyway and keep the exact core as the oracle.
218	* Neutral, because the wire shapes the browser reads keep their names and types. Two fields change what they carry — `series` (above) and `moved_only_by_reweighting` (always false, and deleted at the flip) — and `Verdict.product` becomes always empty, which the browser already handles.

220	### Confirmation
221	
222	**Two oracles, two tolerances, proving two different things.** One alone could not have caught the error measured above: an enumerator built from the core's own tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table, which is exactly what is wrong.
223	
224	1. **`test_the_elimination_is_exact`** — tolerance `1e-9`. Takes the core's **own** yes/no tables and sums the joint by hand, applying **Suppose this is true** as a point and **This happened** as a mask-and-renormalise. Proves the elimination, the supposition surgery and the conditioning arithmetic. Fast, and blind to timing.
225	2. **`test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time`** — tolerance `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened*>>`. Forbidden the core's tables. Built from the arrow's own parameters alone, it enumerates the full joint of event times on maps of four claims or fewer and reads off the chance each claim ever happened. It must run **Suppose this is true** *and* **This happened**, and it must include an impulse arrow and a diamond — a step-shaped chain does not reproduce the error, measured. A working eighty-line version of this enumerator exists as `rt_core.exact_over_times`, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/redteam/`.

227	**And the locality oracle, restated and made stricter:** *cut off from the evidence ⇒ bit for bit.* Today the property test hand-rolls the affected-set rule; under exact elimination the rule is the standard graph separation test, and a claim separated from the evidence must come back byte-identical, not merely close.

267	## Pros and Cons of the Options
268	
269	### A. Repair inside today's engine
270	
271	* Good, because it is the smallest change and touches one file.
272	* Bad, because the first defect's fix costs either the range or thirty times the latency, measured.
273	* Bad, because the second defect has no repair — making the read-day per world makes the settled day random, and the grid, the day-states, retraction and the locality proof are all built on it being fixed.
274	* Bad, because it leaves the third defect, the path product, the clamp in the band, versions with no surviving world, claims that un-resolve, and a number read on one day for a claim phrased *by* that day.
275	* *Two pieces of it are worth doing as insurance if this design slips:* the per-version effective-sample-size warning and the survivor-count divisor, seventeen lines together.
276	
277	### B. Exact inference over event times
278	
279	* Good, because the model is right — the calibration reproduces the two elicited numbers to four places, the answer is grid-independent, and observing a claim gives exact Bayes upstream. **This design adopts the model and rejects only the inference.**
280	* Bad, because measured it is 0.7–7.8 seconds for one range at 20 claims and 58–119 seconds at 30, against a latency budget of 300 ms. It fails its own kill criterion on exactly the maps generation is built to produce.
281	* Bad, because a Hormuz-only prototype cannot see this: seven claims is trivial for every engine here.
282	
283	### C. This design (chosen)
284	
285	* Good, because it is exact for *Suppose this is true* — 4 480 numbers, mean gap `.00007`, 99.8% inside `.005` — and it is fast: `0.5 ms` at 20 claims against `0.7–7.8 s`.
286	* Good, because it keeps the time model on the arrow, which is where the trade reads it.
287	* Good, because locality and the width shares fall out of the arithmetic instead of being maintained.
288	* Bad, because *This happened* is an approximation whose size has to be measured and printed, and the project's second verb is the one it lands on.
289	* Bad, because it changes every number on the map once and costs five to ten sessions.
290	
291	### D. Do nothing
292	
293	* Good, because it costs nothing and nothing breaks today.
294	* Bad, because the thesis card would rest on endings that do not move when half their causes do, and on a second verb that prints the first verb's answer. That is the traceability veto, applied to the product's core claim.
295	
296	## More Information
297	
298	* **Kent's decisions, 2026-09-21**, taken through the question tool over four rounds after two independent midpoint reviews: *an exact core with a sampler on top · keep the time model and make it sound · yes, opening with a spike and a kill criterion · replace the path product with the shift, the joint and the weakest arrow.* Recorded the same evening in the dated decisions note kept locally under `plans/notes/`.
299	* **The evidence.** Four read-only digests of the two reviews and one adversarial pass over the design they produced, all 2026-09-21, kept locally under `plans/analysis/` with their scripts under `plans/analysis/scripts/`. Every measurement in this record is either quoted from one of those reports with its table named, or was re-run on 2026-09-21 by this record's author and is named as such.
300	* **Related records.** ADR-0004 (a supposition is a timed assertion) · ADR-0005 (amended here, not superseded) · ADR-0014 (amended here; its meaning of a range stands) · ADR-0015 (intact) · proposed ADR-0017 (events and states, which this record makes necessary) · proposed ADR-0021 (what version one does not build).

# ADR-0016: A claim's number is the chance it happens by its deadline; whether is solved exactly, when is sampled

> **Written `proposed`, and it must stay `proposed` until a one-session spike has filled the places marked `<<SPIKE: …>>`.** Every one of those is a number nobody has measured yet. Nothing is built against this record until Kent accepts it with those places filled (PRD anti-pattern 13: *do not implement against a `proposed` decision record*).

## Context and Problem Statement

Every tile on the map carries a number, and the sentence beside it says *the chance this claim comes out true by its deadline*. The engine does not compute that. It computes something else — a likelihood read on one particular day — and three defects follow from the gap. All three reproduce on `main` (`48eb562`) today, on the demonstration map, under a test suite that is green at 100% coverage of the pure core.

So: **what does a number on a tile mean, and what arithmetic works it out?**

### The three defects, each with the example that shows it

All three were re-run on 2026-09-21 by the author of this record. The first two scripts are `verify_observe.py` and `verify_trigger_read_day.py`, kept locally under `plans/review2/repro/`; the third is `recheck.py`, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/engine/`. Each prints the numbers quoted here.

**1. Telling the map that something happened never reaches what caused it.**

> A two-claim map — one cause, one effect, both starting at `.30`, one arrow of strength `1.2`. Press **This happened** on the effect. The cause does not move: it still reads `.3000`. Worked out by hand from the map's own two numbers, it should read `.4562`.
> Press **Suppose this is true** on the same claim and the cause reads `.3000` again — the identical number. The product's two verbs are one verb.

On a three-claim chain the miss is larger: after **This happened** on the last claim, the first reads `.3500` where the hand-worked answer is `.4015`, and the middle reads `.4040` where it is `.5971` — a miss of `−.1931`.

*Root cause.* The engine keeps each claim's worked-out likelihood and throws away the coin flip that came out of it (`backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py:1470`). For a claim with no causes that likelihood is the same in every simulated world, so throwing worlds away cannot move it, however much evidence arrives downstream.

**2. The tradeable endings are deaf to half their causes.**

> On the Hormuz map, **Suppose the war-risk insurance premium falls** moves *Brent settles below $68* from `.3925` to `.4759` — eight points — and moves **both** tradeable endings by exactly `0.0000`.
> **Suppose OPEC+ holds its restraint** moves the same Brent claim the other way, `.3925` to `.2197`, and again moves both endings by exactly `0.0000`.

*Root cause.* An arrow reads its source on the day the source's **earliest** incoming arrow lands — one integer doing two different jobs (`propagation.py:842`, `settled[claim_id] = min(arrivals)`, consumed at `:1463`). For the Brent claim that day is day 2. The insurance premium's push lands on day 7 and OPEC+ restraint's on day 5, so both land *inside* the Brent claim's own series — visible on the tile, invisible to everything the tile points at. The series shows it plainly: with the premium supposed, the Brent curve is unchanged through day 6 and only separates from day 7, at `.492` against `.409`.

**3. A claim nobody believes deletes the reader's own assertion.**

> **Suppose the strait is open** on 1 October, then add a claim the map gives one chance in a thousand, carrying an arrow of `−0.01` into it. The tile never reads *Supposed* on any day. Its day-states run `withdrawn, withdrawn, pushed, pushed, …` from day zero, and its number is its own prior, `.30`, throughout.

*Root cause.* A supposition ends on a calendar worked out from the shape of the map — the opposing arrow's source's *settled day*, `max(starts, settled[arrow.source])` (`propagation.py:940-948`) — and the test for which arrows oppose reads only the sign of the push (`:888-895`). Neither the opposing claim's own likelihood nor the size of its push ever enters. A cause at 0.1% with a push that moves nothing wipes out a lever the reader pulled.

### Two more, from the same root

* **A range that is made of coin flips.** Freeze every stated range to a point, so the honest answer is a band of zero width, and run a six-claim chain: two of the six report bands `.0157` and `.0187` wide. Under **This happened** on a three-claim chain the middle claim reports a band **`.1571`** wide with nothing uncertain anywhere on the map.
* **A merged test that enshrines the noise.** `test_an_observation_moves_a_cause_even_when_no_arrow_pushes` (`backend/tests/unit/domain/test_propagation.py:544`) flattens every arrow to no push at all and then requires an observation to move a cause anyway. Under the model the project declares, the correct answer is *no movement*. An artefact is now a contract.

## Decision Drivers

* **The traceability veto** (Kent): no state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule or a cited source. A number that is wrong by `.19` and cannot say so is that state.
* **INV-3, assert is not observe** — *asserting a claim changes nothing upstream of it; observing it may.* Defect 1 makes the two verbs identical, so INV-3 is unenforced on the one screen it exists for.
* **INV-4, locality** — *an intervention changes only what is still connected to its subject in the graph the edit leaves behind.* Whatever replaces the engine must keep this, and should make it easier to prove, not harder.
* **INV-7, honest numbers** — two significant figures with a range. A second figure that moves with the dice is not a second figure.
* **NFR-2, determinism** — the same map, branch and seed give byte-identical worlds.
* **Kent's own direction, 2026-09-21:** *an exact core with a sampler on top*, and *keep the time model and make it sound*.
* **The trade needs event times.** Stack 06 computes the chance a stop is touched before a target on a daily price path. Whatever engine ships has to hand it a sample of *when* each claim came true, not only *whether*.
* **Cost.** Two reviews and five analysts agree the foundations — branches as patches, the validator, locality, the typed wire, replay, the canvas — are sound. Nothing here is allowed to touch them.

## Considered Options

* **A. Repair the three defects inside today's engine.**
* **B. Keep one variable per claim whose value is *the day it first happened*, and solve the network exactly over those days** — the design one of the two reviews proposed.
* **C. This design.** A claim's number becomes *the chance it happens by its deadline*. The arrows bend a **rate** — how likely a claim is to happen on each day — instead of a likelihood read on one day. *When* a cause arrives comes from one forward pass. *Whether* each claim happens is then solved exactly over yes/no truths.
* **D. Do nothing, and ship the thesis on today's numbers.**

Three terms, each once:

* A **rate** (the standard name is a *hazard*) is how likely a claim is to happen on a given day, given it has not happened yet. Add it up over the claim's window and you get the chance it has happened by the end — a **first passage** probability, which is the first day something crosses a line.
* **Variable elimination** is the standard way to solve a sparse network of yes/no claims exactly: multiply the small tables together and sum out one claim at a time, cheapest first. It is exact arithmetic, not a sample.
* **Likelihood weighting** is the sampling alternative to throwing inconsistent worlds away: keep every world and give it a weight saying how well it matches the evidence.

### What each option costs, measured

| | Measured | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **A** leaves the third defect standing, and its fix for the first destroys the range: the within-version spread of a yes/no flag is about `0.25` against an across-version spread of about `0.01`, so the noise correction clamps to zero and every band under **This happened** collapses to a point. Restoring it needs about thirty times more worlds: **66.3 ms → about 2 s** per call | one `propagate` on the fixture today is **66.3 ms** at 2 000 versions × 8 worlds, **8.6 ms** at 250 × 8 | `recheck.py` §5, re-run 2026-09-21 |
| **A**'s fix for the second defect does not exist cheaply: the right day is per world, so the settled day becomes random — and the grid, the day-states, retraction and the locality proof are all built on it being fixed | — | engine digest §3a |
| **B**, on generated 20-claim maps with at most three causes a claim: **0.7–7.8 s** for one range, largest intermediate table **4.8–62.7 million entries**; at 30 claims **58–119 s**, or out of memory. Its own kill criterion — a generated 30-claim map over about one second — fires at the coarsest grid tried | | engine digest §0(2), `ve_cost.py`, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/engine/` |
| **C**, the same networks over yes/no truths with every version on one array axis: **0.5 ms** at 20 claims, **1.7 ms** at 30 | | engine digest §0(2); *the adversarial pass did not re-run the timing* |
| **C**'s accuracy against **B** used as the judge, 140 adversarially generated four-claim maps, tight deadlines, lags up to 70% of each gap, all three arrow shapes, 9 520 compared numbers | table below | red-team report M1, `attack2.py` §B |
| **D** costs nothing and ships a thesis card resting on endings that do not move when half their causes do | — | defect 2 above |

**C's accuracy, by verb:**

| Query | numbers compared | mean gap | 99th percentile | worst | share off by more than `.005` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit | 560 | `.00027` | `.0046` | `.0175` | 0.9% |
| **Suppose this is true** | 4 480 | `.00007` | `.0015` | `.0259` | **0.2%** |
| **This happened** | 4 480 | `.00127` | `.0151` | **`.2043`** | **6.6%** |

**So "exact" is true of *Suppose this is true* and is not true of *This happened*, and this record does not claim otherwise.** The arithmetic is exact; the *table* it is applied to is built from timing worked out before the evidence arrived, and evidence moves *when* a cause happened as well as *whether* it happened. Re-run on 2026-09-21 by the author of this record, the worst map gives exact `.6318` against this design's `.5076` — a gap of **`.1242`** at a fine grid, stable, so not an artefact of the grid. Its shape: three causes, impulse arrows with long lags, and the evidence landing on a claim that is itself a cause of another cause.

Two facts bound it. A plain chain is exact — on a three-claim chain with an observation in the middle, every gap this design makes is `+0.0000` at every half-life tried. And the obvious patch makes it worse: rebuilding the tables from the timing *after* conditioning double-counts the evidence, and on the two worst maps the gaps grow from `+.0338` to `+.0581` and from `+.0352` to `+.0501` (red-team report M1, `attack2.py` §C).

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: **C**, because it is the only option measured to honour both halves of Kent's direction — an exact core, and the time model kept — at a cost that leaves the range, the locality proof and the wire shapes intact, and because it is the only one that hands stack 06 the event times the trade needs.

### What a number means

**A claim's number is the chance it resolves YES by its own deadline.** That is what the sentence on the tile already says. It is not a snapshot read on one day, and **an event that has happened never un-happens**.

### Where the time model lives — unchanged

On the arrow. `strength`, `lag`, `shape` and `half_life` keep their names and their meanings. What changes is what they bend: a **rate** — how likely the claim is to happen on each day — instead of a likelihood read on one day. The claim's number is that rate added up across its window.

One good thing falls out. An impulse's whole area now counts, so the answer no longer depends on where a deadline happens to fall against a half-life. That is the wart record 0014 admitted, and it is gone: impulse arrows with half-lives of one and two days landing four days before a deadline were attacked deliberately and gave gaps of `.0000` to `.0001` (red-team report §4).

*Where the two numbers on an arrow come from is not settled here.* Today the model states an abstract `strength` and our prompt anchors it with a sentence we invented. Kent has decided (2026-09-21) that the claim's own number is asked as *the chance it happens by its deadline if none of the causes on this map happens*, and each arrow as *the chance if this cause happens at the start of the window and no other cause does*, with our code deriving the weight. That change moves what we ask the model, so it lands in the one shape freeze at the end of stack 05 and amends record 0006, not this record.

### How it is worked out — two passes

1. **One forward pass gives *when*.** Causes first, each claim's chance of having happened by each of 12–24 points across its window. A **Suppose this is true** pins its claim to the day it was supposed and the pass is redone. A claim's yes/no table is then its rate averaged over when its causes arrived.
2. **Variable elimination gives *whether*, exactly.** The claims are yes/no, so the whole joint is solved by multiplying the small tables and summing out one claim at a time. **Suppose this is true** replaces a claim's table with a point and cuts its incoming arrows; **This happened** multiplies in an indicator and renormalises. The versions of the map ride along as an array axis, so a whole range is one pass.
3. **The worlds the trade needs are drawn on top:** sample truths from the exact joint, then sample each true claim's arrival day forward. Nothing ever conditions on a time, so no inference over times is needed.

Two properties stop being machinery and become facts. **Locality becomes a theorem** — a claim cut off from the evidence gets its prior back bit for bit, because its factor sums to one. And **the width shares (FR-21, where more homework would pay) become exact** — re-solve with one stated range frozen, one extra solve each.

### The one thing not yet settled: how *This happened* is computed

The spike that opens stack 05 measures three candidates against the enumerator that integrates over event times, on the adversarial maps above.

* **(a) A weighted forward sample.** Draw worlds forward *with times* — the sampler stack 06 needs anyway — and weight each by how well it matches the evidence. It integrates over *when* correctly, so it converges on the right answer; its cost is sampling noise, and only on observation branches. This is Kent's *"exact core with a sampler on top"* read literally, and it is the recommendation going in.
* **(b) Accept the prior-timing tables** and print an observation's numbers to the tolerance measured.
* **(c) Re-cut the yes/no variable per evidence day.** Larger tables; may be exact; may be slow.

**Kill criterion, fixed before the measuring starts:** if no candidate holds `.005` on 99% of the adversarial set inside 300 ms on a 20-claim map, this design is not adopted as it stands and Kent is told with the numbers.

**What the spike must write into this record:**

* `<<SPIKE: which candidate computes *This happened* — (a), (b) or (c) — named, with one sentence saying how it works>>`
* `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *Suppose this is true*>>`
* `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened* — the number that goes into `test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time` and onto the screen's honesty line>>`
* `<<SPIKE: the share of the adversarial set inside that tolerance under *This happened*>>`
* `<<SPIKE: how many versions of the map a range needs, measured — today's 2 000 was chosen for a sampler that no longer exists>>`
* `<<SPIKE: milliseconds for one range on a 20-claim map, and on the seven-claim Hormuz map, against today's 66.3 ms>>`

### If the spike's kill criterion fires

Then this record is not accepted as written, and it becomes the record of an attempt. What survives is still worth having and is re-proposed on its own: the two oracles (they are the missing tests whatever engine ships), the deletion of retraction by calendar, and the path product's replacement. What would then be on the table is option **A** as insurance — the per-version effective-sample-size warning and the survivor-count divisor, seventeen lines together, which fix neither headline defect but stop the band lying — and the honest statement on the thesis card that **This happened** does not reach a cause. Kent is told with the numbers, not with a recommendation.

### What `World.series` now means — the largest change hiding in the smallest field

Today `series` is a per-day likelihood that is allowed to **fall**, and the golden test pins exactly that (`backend/tests/unit/fixtures/test_hormuz_golden.py:117-120`): the supposed strait claim reads `1.0` on day zero, about `.36` on days one and three, and below `.10` on day four — `1.0 → .36 → .36 → <.10`.

**Under "the chance it has happened by day *t*", a series can only rise.** `1.0 → .36` is arithmetically impossible. That test cannot survive; what replaces it is the events-and-states reading of the same branch, which is proposed record 0017's to write.

Three consequences, stated so nobody is surprised at the flip:

* **An event's series is a rising curve.** The field keeps its name and its type. The forward pass runs at 12–24 points and the browser draws up to 180 days (`propagation.py:110`, `SERIES_CAP = 180`), so the days between grid points are read off the same added-up rate rather than re-solved. `<<SPIKE: the cost of filling 180 displayed days from a 12–24 point forward pass, in milliseconds on a 20-claim map>>`
* **`DeltaRow.peak_delta` and `at_day` keep their arithmetic and lose their story.** They were written for a curve that "shows up for a fortnight and then unwinds" (`backend/src/katalyst/domain/diff.py:239-252`). For an event, both worlds' curves rise, so `at_day` no longer marks a spike that unwinds. Whether it still lands anywhere but the last day the series carries is a fact the flip's generated numbers file will state; this record does not assert it. A curve that falls comes back with record 0017's **states**.
* **The golden test's domino assertion is restated.** `test_hormuz_golden.py:81` pins that the Brent series rises between day one and day two — *what already fell stays fallen*. Under a rising curve that passes by construction and proves nothing. The domino is instead proved by comparing the two branches on the same day.

### A supposed claim's stored `p = 1.0` stays

The first draft of this design removed it, on the grounds that the path product was its only reader. It is not. Three readers, all live:

* `backend/src/katalyst/domain/diff.py:817-818` reads it for every change row's *before* and *after*.
* `backend/src/katalyst/domain/diff.py:460` reads it to choose which way to flip a claim in the sensitivity sweep.
* `frontend/src/world/apiSource.ts:263` builds the model belief the tile draws from it.

And `Belief.p` is a plain number with no gap allowed (`backend/src/katalyst/domain/belief.py:39-45`), so removing it is a wire break. **It stays.** The tile still shows the word *Supposed* rather than the number, exactly as record 0014 decided.

### Chains are worked out, not multiplied — the path product's replacement

This is Kent's decision of 2026-09-21 and it rides here because it needs the exact core to exist.

**Why the product goes.** Multiplying likelihoods along a route is not the chance of anything once two claims on the map share a cause. Check it in one line: if a second claim is true exactly when the first is, and both stand at `.5`, the product of the route says `.25`; the chance that every step goes right is `.5`. The product is also read at a different day for every claim on the route, which is the wart record 0014 admitted at its section E.

**What replaces it**, three quantities, each a probability or a difference of probabilities, each one or two extra solves:

| | What it is |
|---|---|
| **the shift** | how much the hypothesis moves the destination: the destination's chance with the hypothesis supposed true, minus its chance with the hypothesis supposed false |
| **the joint** | the chance every step on the named route goes right — a real joint, from one elimination that keeps the route |
| **the weakest arrow** | which single arrow carries most of the shift, and how much of the shift goes with it |

What the Verify door then says, *in an illustrative shape only — the real numbers come from the engine at the flip and are owned by the generated numbers file*:

> *"Reopening moves the Brent claim by 32 points, from .24 to .56. Every step on the best-backed route goes right in 19% of worlds. The arrow carrying most of that shift is 'reopening → shipping recovers'; delete it and 71% of the effect goes."*

**INV-8 becomes:** *"Chains are worked out, not multiplied. Any displayed path shows the shift the hypothesis makes to its destination, the chance every step on it goes right computed as a joint, and which single arrow carries most of the shift."* FR-11, which requires *"the product of link probabilities beside the narrative headline"*, is rewritten to match. Both edits are listed for the pull request that carries this record.

The multiplication itself is deleted from `backend/src/katalyst/engine/verify.py:139-167`. It is a server-only change: the browser already renders the absence and never reads the server's product (`frontend/src/world/apiSource.ts:272`, `frontend/src/world/fromTheServer.ts:251`, both hard-coding `NO_PATH_PRODUCT`).

### What this record amends, sentence by sentence

**It amends ADR-0005 without superseding it.** These sentences change:

* The aggregation formula — *"log-odds P(child, t) = log-odds(prior_child) + sum over active links of strength × shape(t − t_parent)"* and the line under it beginning *"In words: start from the child's own base likelihood…"*. The arrows still add, and they still add on a scale where independent pushes add instead of multiplying; what they add to is a **rate** across the window rather than a likelihood on one day.
* *"Execution is Monte Carlo — thousands of random simulations whose spread is the answer. Draw `N` seeded worlds (default 10 000). In each, every proposition is sampled parents-first from its aggregated log-odds."* — replaced by the two passes above. Worlds still exist; they are drawn from the exact answer rather than being the answer.
* *"learning fixes a value and keeps only the draws consistent with it (warn loudly when fewer than about 2% survive)"* and the paragraph beginning *"Keeping only the consistent draws is why learning reaches further than asserting…"* — the **rule** stands (observing a claim may move its causes; supposing it may not, INV-3) and the **mechanism** changes: nothing is thrown away, and there is nothing to starve. The affected sets of the 2026-09-17 amendment are untouched.
* *"A belief is the share of worlds in which the proposition came out true"* — it is the chance the claim happens by its deadline, worked out exactly.
* The `mode` row of the link-fields table, the consequence bullet beginning *"Good, because `trigger` versus `sustain` makes the Hormuz-then-strike branch behave correctly"*, and the two confirmation tests `test_trigger_persists_after_parent_reset` and `test_sustain_retracts_when_parent_removed` — **proposed record 0017 owns these**, and this record does not touch them.

**Standing untouched in ADR-0005:** the arrow's fields and their meanings; one number and one sentence per arrow; two significant figures with the interval; and every rejected option — per-combination tables, scenario trees, Markov steady states, role-played simulation, model narration.

**It amends ADR-0014 without superseding it.** Section B's *machinery* changes and its *meaning* does not: `lo` and `hi` stay the 10th and 90th percentiles of the likelihood itself, and a wide range still never means the event is more volatile. What goes is the eight-worlds-per-version inner loop, the noise-correction formula and its glossary, and section F entirely — the reject-the-inconsistent-worlds rule, the survival weighting, and the starve warning. The band becomes the 10th and 90th percentiles of exact answers across versions, with no correction, because there is no inner noise to correct. Section E's *"known wart"* paragraph goes with the path product. Section D's 90% bar and `.005` floor stand; its 2026-09-17 amendment about survival weights becomes vacuous, and `moved_only_by_reweighting` becomes always false. The dated amendment appended to record 0014 in this pull request states all of it.

**ADR-0015 survives intact.** `lo` and `hi` keep exactly the meaning it protects, and nothing here asks a claim twice.

### Consequences

* Good, because the number on a tile finally answers the sentence beside it, and **This happened** does something.
* Good, because supposing any cause on the Hormuz map now moves what that cause points at — defect 2 was the flagship demonstration's quietest failure.
* Good, because locality stops being careful bookkeeping and becomes a property of the arithmetic, and the oracle that checks it can get **stricter**.
* Good, because the range stops carrying coin-flip width: with every stated range frozen to a point, the band is zero by construction rather than within a tolerance.
* Good, because the trade in stack 06 gets a forward sample of *when*, which nothing today produces.
* Bad, because **every number on the map changes once**. That is why the flip is a pull request of its own whose review is the diff of one generated file.
* Bad, because *This happened* is exact arithmetic on a table built from timing worked out before the evidence — accurate to `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened*>>` and not to machine precision — and the screen prints two significant figures. Whatever the spike returns, the second figure's honesty is stated in the Inspector in words.
* Bad, because the induced width of a *generated* map has never been measured: the one real generated map is a tree. Mitigation: at width 7 the exact core is `1.7 ms` on a 30-claim map, four orders of magnitude of headroom; if a pathological map ever appears, fall back to the forward sampler stack 06 uses anyway and keep the exact core as the oracle.
* Neutral, because the wire shapes the browser reads keep their names and types. Two fields change what they carry — `series` (above) and `moved_only_by_reweighting` (always false, and deleted at the flip) — and `Verdict.product` becomes always empty, which the browser already handles.

### Confirmation

**Two oracles, two tolerances, proving two different things.** One alone could not have caught the error measured above: an enumerator built from the core's own tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table, which is exactly what is wrong.

1. **`test_the_elimination_is_exact`** — tolerance `1e-9`. Takes the core's **own** yes/no tables and sums the joint by hand, applying **Suppose this is true** as a point and **This happened** as a mask-and-renormalise. Proves the elimination, the supposition surgery and the conditioning arithmetic. Fast, and blind to timing.
2. **`test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time`** — tolerance `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened*>>`. Forbidden the core's tables. Built from the arrow's own parameters alone, it enumerates the full joint of event times on maps of four claims or fewer and reads off the chance each claim ever happened. It must run **Suppose this is true** *and* **This happened**, and it must include an impulse arrow and a diamond — a step-shaped chain does not reproduce the error, measured. A working eighty-line version of this enumerator exists as `rt_core.exact_over_times`, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/redteam/`.

**And the locality oracle, restated and made stricter:** *cut off from the evidence ⇒ bit for bit.* Today the property test hand-rolls the affected-set rule; under exact elimination the rule is the standard graph separation test, and a claim separated from the evidence must come back byte-identical, not merely close.

Also: `test_an_observation_moves_a_cause_even_when_no_arrow_pushes` is **reversed** into an assertion of invariance, and `test_band_is_not_sampling_noise` survives and tightens to zero width exactly.

### How it lands, so `main` is never red and the canvas never shows nonsense

| Step | Contents | `main` after |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | The two oracles and their enumerators. The failing cases marked strictly expected-to-fail, by name, each naming the defect it documents. Reverse the noise-enshrining test. | Green. Two tests documenting two defects. |
| **2** | The new core beside the old, behind a flag, **default unchanged**. Both oracles run against both engines. | Green. **Every screen still shows today's numbers.** |
| **3** | **The flip, alone.** The default changes; Hormuz is re-derived; the generated numbers file is regenerated — **its diff is the complete and reviewable statement of which numbers moved**. The sampler, the noise correction, the version weights and `moved_only_by_reweighting` go; `diff.py` moves over; the browser's two readers and its *"eight worlds under each"* sentence are corrected. | Green. Every number changes **once**, atomically. |
| **4** | Separately: the Verify door's three quantities; and proposed record 0017's events and states. | Green. |

**The flip's reviewable statement is the generated numbers file's diff.** One committed file owns every number the worked example quotes; the build regenerates it and fails on a difference. That file must exist *before* step 3, or the flip's pull request also carries a sweep of several hundred numbers across the chapters and nobody can review it.

### Honest cost

Five to seven sessions is the floor for this record's work alone; nine or ten once record 0017's events and states are counted (the adversarial pass's bottom-up estimate, 2026-09-21; a session is about three focused hours). The first draft said three, scoped to one file. What that missed, all verified on `main`:

* **`diff.py`** — 1 459 lines, of which the version weights, the reweighting flag, the band import, the sensitivity sweep's reading of retractions and the ranked list's reading of `series` all die or change.
* **The browser**, budgeted at zero: two rendering readers of the reweighting flag; the retraction badge, whose height is baked into the tile's geometry; and the provenance sentence that prints *"…worlds under each"* (`frontend/src/world/apiSource.ts:228`), which becomes a false statement about an engine with no inner loop.
* **Tests** — **34 of `test_propagation.py`'s 46** touch the dying machinery (46 confirmed by count on `main`).
* **The locality oracle**, which must be rewritten and should get stricter.
* **About 400 numeric literals** across the two multiverse chapters, all of which move at once — which is what the generated numbers file is for.

For calibration: commit `d9c853e` (pull request #38) fixed **one** defect class, kept every wire meaning, and cost **1 335 insertions across 12 files**. This is larger.

## Open for Kent

**1. What the screen says about *This happened*'s tolerance.** The spike returns a number; the reader has to be told something true.

* *Recommended:* one sentence in the Inspector, on an observation branch only — *"learning moves numbers upstream; ours are within `<<SPIKE: the measured tolerance for *This happened*>>` of the exact answer on maps this size."* Cost: one sentence, one place, and it is only shown where it applies.
* Alternative: say it once on the honesty line for every world. Cheaper to build, and it puts a caveat on screens the caveat is not about.
* Alternative: say nothing and rely on the record. Cheapest, and it is the traceability veto.

**2. How many versions a range gets.** Today it is 2 000, chosen for a sampler that no longer exists; the engine digest suggests about 200 is enough once the inner answers are exact.

* *Recommended:* take the spike's measured number, whatever it is, and write it here with the measurement beside it.
* Alternative: keep 2 000 regardless, because it is what record 0014 specifies. Costs latency for nothing.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### A. Repair inside today's engine

* Good, because it is the smallest change and touches one file.
* Bad, because the first defect's fix costs either the range or thirty times the latency, measured.
* Bad, because the second defect has no repair — making the read-day per world makes the settled day random, and the grid, the day-states, retraction and the locality proof are all built on it being fixed.
* Bad, because it leaves the third defect, the path product, the clamp in the band, versions with no surviving world, claims that un-resolve, and a number read on one day for a claim phrased *by* that day.
* *Two pieces of it are worth doing as insurance if this design slips:* the per-version effective-sample-size warning and the survivor-count divisor, seventeen lines together.

### B. Exact inference over event times

* Good, because the model is right — the calibration reproduces the two elicited numbers to four places, the answer is grid-independent, and observing a claim gives exact Bayes upstream. **This design adopts the model and rejects only the inference.**
* Bad, because measured it is 0.7–7.8 seconds for one range at 20 claims and 58–119 seconds at 30, against a latency budget of 300 ms. It fails its own kill criterion on exactly the maps generation is built to produce.
* Bad, because a Hormuz-only prototype cannot see this: seven claims is trivial for every engine here.

### C. This design (chosen)

* Good, because it is exact for *Suppose this is true* — 4 480 numbers, mean gap `.00007`, 99.8% inside `.005` — and it is fast: `0.5 ms` at 20 claims against `0.7–7.8 s`.
* Good, because it keeps the time model on the arrow, which is where the trade reads it.
* Good, because locality and the width shares fall out of the arithmetic instead of being maintained.
* Bad, because *This happened* is an approximation whose size has to be measured and printed, and the project's second verb is the one it lands on.
* Bad, because it changes every number on the map once and costs five to ten sessions.

### D. Do nothing

* Good, because it costs nothing and nothing breaks today.
* Bad, because the thesis card would rest on endings that do not move when half their causes do, and on a second verb that prints the first verb's answer. That is the traceability veto, applied to the product's core claim.

## More Information

* **Kent's decisions, 2026-09-21**, taken through the question tool over four rounds after two independent midpoint reviews: *an exact core with a sampler on top · keep the time model and make it sound · yes, opening with a spike and a kill criterion · replace the path product with the shift, the joint and the weakest arrow.* Recorded the same evening in the dated decisions note kept locally under `plans/notes/`.
* **The evidence.** Four read-only digests of the two reviews and one adversarial pass over the design they produced, all 2026-09-21, kept locally under `plans/analysis/` with their scripts under `plans/analysis/scripts/`. Every measurement in this record is either quoted from one of those reports with its table named, or was re-run on 2026-09-21 by this record's author and is named as such.
* **Related records.** ADR-0004 (a supposition is a timed assertion) · ADR-0005 (amended here, not superseded) · ADR-0014 (amended here; its meaning of a range stands) · ADR-0015 (intact) · proposed ADR-0017 (events and states, which this record makes necessary) · proposed ADR-0021 (what version one does not build).
* **Chapters this rewrites.** `spec/multiverse/propagation.md` and `spec/multiverse/diff.md`, in the pull request that carries this record.
* Judea Pearl's causal hierarchy — we work at its second level, intervention, not the third: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/pearl-s-causal-hierarchy-pch

13	# ADR-0017: A claim is an event or a state; nothing retracts itself
14	
15	> **Written `proposed`.** It depends on proposed record 0016 being accepted — it exists because that record deletes something — and it carries `<<SPIKE: …>>` places that a one-session spike is measuring now. Nothing is built against it until Kent accepts it with those places filled.
16	
17	## Context and Problem Statement
18	
19	Record 0005 gives every arrow a `mode`. A **`trigger`** arrow is a domino: it fires when its cause becomes true, and standing the cause back up later does not undo it. A **`sustain`** arrow is a desk holding an apple: the effect holds only while the cause holds, and take the cause away and the effect falls. Record 0005 calls that pair *"the best idea in the brainstorm"*, and Kent asked for it to be kept.
20	
21	Proposed record 0016 deletes it — not deliberately, as a side effect. Under that record a claim's number is *the chance it has happened by day t*, and something that has happened never un-happens. The moment that is true, the quantity a `sustain` arrow reads (its cause's truth, read on each day) and the quantity a `trigger` arrow reads (whether its cause has fired) are **the same thing**.
22	
23	**Measured.** In today's code a `sustain` arrow pushes with the cause's truth read on every day and a `trigger` arrow with a single fired-or-not flag per world (`backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py:1431-1434`). They differ for exactly one reason: today a claim can **un-resolve** when an impulse fades (`:1444`) — which is the defect proposed record 0016 removes on purpose. Build both under first passage and they are not close, they are the same number: `0.442471` and `0.442471` on the map the check builds, because the two arrays are the same array. `mode` becomes dead data, fully determined by `shape`. (Re-run on 2026-09-21 by this record's author; the check is `attack3.py` section B, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/redteam/`.)
24	
25	The only mechanism in the product that can make a true claim untrue is **automatic retraction** — the rule of record 0014, which ends a supposition on a calendar worked out from the shape of the map. That rule is itself one of the three defects proposed record 0016 exists to fix. It cannot be the thing that saves `sustain`.
26	
27	So: **does a `sustain` arrow survive, and if so, what does it leave?** The question is not optional and "leave it as it is" is not on the list.
28	
29	### The second reason, which is the brief's own sentence
30	
31	The brief's example is *"the Strait of Hormuz opened but Iran was struck the next day."* That asks for a world in which **both things happened**. Today the strike retracts the opening: Monday's event un-happens because of Tuesday's news, and the flagship branch's headline is a claim the reader asserted being deleted by a claim the reader inserted.
32	
33	And the deletion fires on a schedule, not on anything real. Suppose the strait is open on 1 October, then add a claim the map gives one chance in a thousand, carrying an arrow of `−0.01` into it: the tile never reads *Supposed* on any day — its day-states run `withdrawn, withdrawn, pushed, pushed, …` from day zero and its number is its own prior throughout (re-run 2026-09-21; `recheck.py` section 1, kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/engine/`).
34	
35	## Decision Drivers
36	
37	* **Record 0005's best idea, and Kent's instruction to keep it.** Whatever ships must either keep the distinction or say plainly that it is gone.
38	* **The brief's own sentence must come out right.** Both events stand.
39	* **The traceability veto** (Kent): no state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule or a cited source. A supposition deleted by a cause nobody believes is that state.
40	* **INV-3, assert is not observe** — *supposing a claim changes nothing upstream of it.* Deleting the supposition is a stronger move than anything INV-3 contemplates.
41	* **Pay once** (Kent, 2026-09-21): everything that changes what we ask the model lands in one freeze, and the four examples are recorded once after it.
42	* **The canvas is meant to be settling down.** A change here is worth having only if it is mostly *deletion*.
43	
44	## Considered Options
45	
46	The three Kent was offered on 2026-09-21, in the words they were put in:
47	
48	* **(i) Events and states.** A claim is an **event** (once it has happened, it has happened) or a **state** (it holds over a stretch of time and can stop holding). A `sustain` arrow may only leave a state. Automatic retraction is deleted.
49	* **(ii) Events only; a sustained push is two arrows** — one from the event that starts it, and an inhibiting arrow from the event that ends it. Same arithmetic, one validity rule, one sentence in the prompt, no new field. `mode` and the word *sustain* leave the vocabulary.
50	* **(iii) Keep today's snapshot meaning, for states only.** Two meanings of a number on one map.
51	
52	**Kent chose (i) on 2026-09-21.**
53	
54	## Decision Outcome
55	
56	Chosen option: **"(i) Events and states"**, because it is the only one of the three under which the brief's own example sentence comes out right — both events stand, and what falls is the thing everything downstream actually depended on — and because it is the only one that gives record 0005's best idea something real to be about.
57	
58	### What a claim carries
59	
60	One new field on a claim, `persistence`, with two values:
61	
62	| | What it means | Hormuz |
63	|---|---|---|
64	| **event** | Once it has happened, it has happened. Its number is the chance it happens by its deadline, and its curve only rises. | *The Strait of Hormuz reopens to unrestricted commercial transit.* *A confirmed military strike on Iranian territory.* |
65	| **state** | It holds over a stretch of time, and it can stop holding. | *The strait stays open to commercial transit through 1 November.* |
66	
67	A `sustain` arrow may leave **only** a state. That is the whole of the rule, and it is what gives the word *sustain* a job again: a state can stop, so an effect that holds only while its cause holds has something to stop with.
68	
69	**What a state's number means in the arithmetic is not settled here.** A parallel measurement is running now. A state that holds over an interval is not one yes/no fact: four maps in which *"did it ever hold?"* is YES in every row, differing only in when the state switched on and off, give the claim it sustains `.8269`, `.1483`, `.1934` and `.2151` — about `.68` of probability spread across maps that a single yes/no cannot tell apart (re-run 2026-09-21; `attack3.py` section C). So a state needs an on-time and an off-time, and the questions below are measured, not guessed:
70	
71	* `<<SPIKE: what a state claim's number answers, in the one sentence the tile will print — "it holds on its deadline", "it ever held", or something else>>`
72	* `<<SPIKE: how a state's on-time and off-time are represented, and how many variables in the solve a state claim costs>>`
73	* `<<SPIKE: the cost of a state claim — milliseconds for one range on a 20-claim map carrying state claims, against the same map with none>>`
74	
75	### The Hormuz strike, before and after, in the words on screen
76	
77	**Today**, pinned by the golden test (`backend/tests/unit/fixtures/test_hormuz_golden.py:110-123`): the supposed strait claim reads **Supposed** on day zero, then **withdrawn** on days one to three and **pushed** from day four, and the tile carries the badge
78	
79	> **Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory"**
80	
81	The world carries one retraction naming the strike as the thing that revoked the reader's own supposition. The reader supposed a thing; the product deleted it.
82	
83	**After this record**, the same branch reads as three lines that are all true at once:
84	
85	> *the strait opened* — **Supposed · Oct 1**
86	> *a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory* — **Added**
87	> *the strait stays open to commercial transit through 1 November* — a number, which the strike lowers
88	> *Brent settles below $68* — a number, which follows the state down
89	
90	*(Shape only. The numbers come from the engine when the flip lands, and the generated numbers file owns them.)* Both events stand. Nothing on the map contradicts the reader. What moves is the state everything downstream was resting on, which is the claim the reader should have been watching all along.
91	
92	### What is deleted
93	
94	All of this goes, and it is the reason the change is worth its cost — it is removal, not another guard on a canvas that is meant to be settling down.
95	
96	* **The `Retracted · date · by "…"` badge.** `spec/vocabulary.md` calls it the one *derived* badge, the only one no button produces. It goes, and so does its entry there; its height is baked into the tile's geometry, which comes back.
97	* **Two of the four day-states.** `SeriesState` is `sampled · supposed · withdrawn · pushed` (`propagation.py:90`); `withdrawn` and `pushed` go and the first two remain. This is cheap: the browser has exactly one live reader of the day-states and it tests for `"supposed"` alone (`frontend/src/world/apiSource.ts:194`, checked on `main`).
98	* **Retraction by calendar, entirely** — the test for which arrows oppose a supposition, the undermining half of the rule that lays out a supposition's spells, the code that builds the retractions, and the `Retraction` model on the wire (`propagation.py:147`, `:888-895`, `:940-948`, `:962`).
99	* **With it, the third defect.** There is no schedule left to fire, so no claim the map gives a thousand-to-one chance can delete anything.
100	* **UX-14** as written — *"a claim the user supposed true, and that a later edit in the same branch has pushed back down, never renders as plainly true… its tile carries both states in order"* — describes a thing that no longer happens. It is replaced by a requirement about states: a claim that stops holding says when it stopped and what stopped it. The replacement wording is listed for the pull request that carries this record.
101	
102	**This reverses decision A of record 0014** — *"a supposition is a hard fact in every simulated world, and it ends on the day the cause of the first live arrow pushing against it becomes true"* — and its three-state table, and its two confirmation tests `test_retraction_dates_from_the_cause_not_the_push` and the Hormuz golden series. **What stands from record 0014:** a supposition is a hard fact in every world *while it holds*; the tile shows the word **Supposed · date** and never a number. What changes is that nothing ends it but another edit.
103	
104	**It amends ADR-0005's `mode` table** — the row reading *"`sustain` — the effect holds only while the parent holds; remove the parent and it retracts"* now reads *"…only while the parent holds; a `sustain` arrow may leave only a state, because only a state can stop"*. Its consequence bullet about the Hormuz-then-strike branch is restated: the pair works, and the thing it works on is a state.
105	
106	### The new rules the map must obey
107	
108	1. **A `sustain` arrow may only leave a claim whose `persistence` is `state`.** A twenty-first violation code, `sustain_without_a_state`, in the pattern of the twenty that exist (`documented_without_source`, `market_without_payoff`, `reflexive_without_lag`). Rejected, never repaired — turning the arrow into a `trigger` silently would be our code deciding what the model meant.
109	2. **Every claim says which kind it is.** No code in the pure core can read a claim's sentence and decide whether it names an event or a state; that judgement is the model's, which is why this field moves what we ask for.
110	
111	### This field rides the one shape freeze, and record 0017 must be accepted before that freeze is written
112	
113	Adding `persistence` to what the model answers moves the **prompt fingerprint** — the hash that says a recording was made by the program that is running now. Measured by the adversarial pass on 2026-09-21: `main` hashes to `1c224cc3…`, and with `persistence` added to the claim proposal it hashes to `1e80b47b…`. A moved fingerprint makes every committed recording stale.
114	
115	Worse, and measured by this record's author on 2026-09-21 against the recording committed on the stack-04 recordings branch: that recording carries **19 accepted arrows, 6 of them `sustain`, and all six leave claims whose `kind` is `event`**. With the validity rule above in force, **all six become illegal.** So:
116	
117	* `persistence` and its rule land **only** in stack 05's shape freeze, with the re-recording in the same pull request — never in a pull request that merges before the new recordings do, or `main` is green over a map its own validator would refuse.
118	* **This record therefore has to be accepted before the freeze is written**, not merged alongside it.
119	
120	Everything else in this record — the retraction deletion, the two day-states, the badge — has no model in it and can land with the engine flip.
121	
122	### Consequences
123	
124	* Good, because the brief's own sentence finally comes out right, and the product stops deleting things the reader typed.
125	* Good, because it is mostly deletion: about 250 lines out of the backend and 120 out of the browser against about 60 added for the field and its rule (engine digest section 5.3, 2026-09-21). Set against those figures, a state's on-and-off representation has not been priced — see the spike tokens above.
126	* Good, because record 0005's best idea keeps its meaning instead of quietly becoming a synonym.
127	* Good, because the third defect dies with the schedule that caused it.
128	* Bad, because the model has to make a judgement it has never been asked for, and nothing in our code can check it. A claim marked `event` that is really a state will simply never stop holding, and the only signal is a reader reading the sentence.
129	* Bad, because it adds a claim to the Hormuz map — *the strait stays open through 1 November* — and every number downstream of the strait moves again for that reason as well as for the engine's.
130	* Bad, because a state costs more in the solve than an event, by an amount nobody has measured yet.
131	* Neutral, because the canvas loses a badge and two colours and gains nothing to draw.
132	
133	### Confirmation
134	
135	* `test_a_sustain_arrow_must_leave_a_state` — the validator refuses a `sustain` arrow out of an event, with its own sentence, and repairs nothing.
136	* `test_both_events_stand_through_the_strike` — on the Hormuz strike branch, the supposed opening reads **Supposed** on every day of the window and the strike reads as having happened; neither is withdrawn, and the world carries no retraction because the model no longer exists.
137	* `test_the_state_is_what_falls` — on the same branch, the state claim's number is lower than in the base world, and so is every claim it sustains. Directions and orderings, never typed-in values.
138	* `test_a_supposition_is_not_ended_by_a_cause_nobody_believes` — the reproduction above, turned into a test: inserting a claim at `.001` with a `−0.01` arrow into a supposed claim leaves it **Supposed** on every day.
139	* `grep -rn "Retraction\|withdrawn\|pushed" backend/src frontend/src` finds nothing outside history.
140	* The two oracles of proposed record 0016 run over maps that carry state claims as well as events, so the tolerance they measure covers both.
141	
142	## Open for Kent
143	
144	**1. The field's name.** `persistence: event | state` collides in a reader's mind with something that already exists: a claim's `kind` is one of `hypothesis · event · market · not_tradeable`. Under this record a `market` claim would carry `persistence: event`, and a claim of `kind: event` could carry `persistence: state` — the word *event* would mean two different things one field apart, on the same tile, in the same Inspector. This record is written with `persistence` throughout; every use of it reads as `<<SPIKE: the field's name, once Kent has chosen>>`.
145	
146	* *Recommended:* keep `persistence` and rename its **values** so the collision disappears — `persistence: once | while`, read as *"once it happens it stays"* and *"only while it holds"*. Cost: nothing in code; two words in the prompt and three sentences in the chapters. It also reads correctly beside `mode: trigger | sustain`, which is the distinction it is really about.
147	* Alternative: keep `persistence: event | state` as proposed. Cost: nothing to build, and a word that means two things on one tile.
148	* Alternative: rename the field instead — `holds: once | while`, or `kind_of_truth`. Cost: the same, and `persistence` is the word both reviews and the design page already use, so every note would have to be reread.
149	
150	**2. Whether a hand-written map may leave the field out.** The model always states it; a fixture is written by a person.
151	
152	* *Recommended:* no default — every claim, hand-written or generated, says which it is. Cost: one line in each of the seven Hormuz claims and in the property-test builders. It matches *reject, never repair*: a map that does not say cannot be guessed at.
153	* Alternative: default to `event`. Cost: nothing today, and the first hand-written state claim someone forgets to mark is a claim that silently never stops holding.
154	
155	## Pros and Cons of the Options
156	
157	### (i) Events and states (chosen)
158	
159	* Good, because *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck"* leaves both events standing and lowers the state everything downstream depends on — which is what the brief asks for and what a trader would actually watch.
160	* Good, because `sustain` gets its meaning back rather than becoming a synonym for `step`.
161	* Good, because automatic retraction — the rule that lets a claim nobody believes delete a reader's assertion — is deleted rather than patched.
162	* Bad, because it is the most expensive of the three: a new field the model must state, a new validity rule, a new claim on the fixture, and a state's on-and-off representation in the solve.
163	* Bad, because it moves the prompt fingerprint, so it is locked to the one paid re-recording.
164	
165	### (ii) Events only; a sustained push is two arrows
166	
167	* Good, because it reproduces `sustain` exactly under first passage — an arrow from the event that starts the push and an inhibiting arrow from the event that ends it — at the cost of one validity rule and one sentence in the prompt.
168	* Good, because it adds no field, so it does not move the fingerprint and does not wait for the freeze. It is the cheapest sound option.
169	* Bad, because `mode` and the word *sustain* leave the vocabulary, and record 0005's best idea becomes a modelling convention rather than a thing the product knows about.
170	* Bad, because the reader has to know to draw two arrows for one mechanism, and nothing on screen says so.
171	
172	### (iii) Keep today's snapshot meaning for states only
173	
174	* Good, because nothing in the engine changes for those claims.
175	* Bad, because two claims side by side on one map would answer two different questions with one number in the same place, which is the thing two significant figures and a range exist to prevent.
176	
177	## More Information
178	
179	* **Kent's decision, 2026-09-21**, taken through the question tool: *"Events and states. Automatic retraction is deleted — 'Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck' leaves both events standing; the strike lowers the state the strait stays open through 1 November. Reverses record 0014, decision A. The model says which kind each claim is, so `persistence` rides the one shape freeze."* Recorded the same evening in the dated decisions note kept locally under `plans/notes/`.
180	* **The measurements.** The `sustain`-equals-`trigger` identity, the four-map spread that shows a state is not one yes/no fact, and the supposition voided by a claim at `.001` were all re-run on 2026-09-21 by this record's author, from scripts kept locally under `plans/analysis/scripts/`. The fingerprint pair and the count of `sustain` arrows in the committed recording are quoted from the adversarial pass of the same date, and the arrow count was re-counted independently: 19 accepted arrows, 6 `sustain`, 3 `impulse`, all six `sustain` arrows leaving claims of `kind: event`.
181	* **Related records.** Proposed ADR-0016 (which this record exists because of) · ADR-0005 (its `mode` table amended here) · ADR-0014 (its decision A reversed here) · ADR-0003 (the model proposes, our code disposes — which is why `persistence` is stated by the model and checked by us) · ADR-0006 (what we ask the model, amended at the freeze) · ADR-0012 (a recording is the real stream played back, which is why the six illegal arrows matter).
